chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
title: Racial segregation answered with respect and upbringing
summary: Asked how musicians reacted to segregation, Crawford says they demanded respect, as his grandparents, teachers and Lunceford taught him.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: MR. CRAWFORD: -- carried myself in a respectful way
Now, when you say you were with some rough teenagers, what do you mean?

You know, little neighborhood kids that you played with. You know, I remember when I was a kid, I was playing with the fellows, neighborhood kids. We had a well in our back yard, old fashioned well. We didn't have no telephone, running water or nothing like that, heat and electrical (inaudible), and those kids used to come all the way to my house to drink that ice cold well water. And I mean it was good, heavy, hit your belly and knock your kneecap off.
Yeah, I'm telling you, and I love -- that's why I'm a great water drinker now.
Now, you were saying that you -- you were just saying that, regardless of how much -- how rough the people were around you, that you always were a mannerable person.
How did the musicians react to the racial situation in the thirties?

How did they react? What could they do about it? We tried to do everything in our power to make us look nice and appear nice and respect people, which I was always taught. I never will forget, "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you." I'll never forget that, and I've done that. I've never been arrested in my life; I don't know what the inside of a jail look like. Never in my life have I been arrested, and I don't know what the inside of a jail look like. That's why; that little wording there, "Do unto others as you have them do unto you." CROUCH: So then, the musicians reacted to the .... CRAWFORD: Segregation. CROUCH: Segregation by trying to carry themselves ... CRAWFORD: Demanding your respect. That's what I was brought up to do by my non-educated grandparents. And in high school, we had some strict teachers there; they were like in society, you know what I'm speaking. For me, I was born in Bear Wallow, and I was with some rough teenagers, but I still carried myself in a xx respectful way.
And this was -- this was put upon you --

Even right here -- but don't get -- don't get out of line, though, you know. Rouse my dandruff, I'm coming out and going tell them. I don't give a darn whether they're Black, white, chicken chile or Chinaman.
And that's a fact. Oh, I've been aroused. I know, I'm going tell them.
So now, do you say that you were prepared by your grandparents, your teachers and Jimmie Lunsford to conduct yourself, carry yourself in a respectful, neat --
-- and be punctual, be on time.
Oh, yeah. That was a must.
